title: Spring: pagination, idempotency, versioning and GraphQL
description: Spring Data paging, keyset queries, idempotency keys, API deprecation headers, conditional GET and Spring for GraphQL batching.
source: Spring Data JPA documentation (Page, Slice, Pageable, scrolling); Spring Web MVC documentation (ShallowEtagHeaderFilter); RFC 9745 and RFC 8594; GraphQL specification; Spring for GraphQL documentation (@SchemaMapping, @BatchMapping); Stripe idempotency documentation; Use The Index, Luke
seriesDescription: Spring Boot structure and DI, REST and validation, error handling, filters, async, API design, jobs and health. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: A Spring Data `PageRequest.of(3, 20)` is used (page index is zero-based). How many rows does the database skip with `OFFSET`?
questions.explanation: offset = `page x size = 3 x 20 = 60`, i.e. the 4th page. Pages in Spring Data start at 0, a common off-by-one trap.

questions.prompt: A Spring Data repository returns a `Page` for `PageRequest.of(0, 25)`, and the table holds 130 matching rows. What does `page.getTotalPages()` return?
questions.explanation: ceil(130 / 25) = ceil(5.2) = 6; the last page holds 5 rows. `Page` knows the total because it runs an extra `COUNT` query, which `Slice` avoids.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Returning `Page<T>` from a Spring Data repository avoids a separate `COUNT` query.
questions.reason: `Slice<T>` avoids the count query by fetching one extra row to learn whether a next page exists.

whys.d: Correct: Page<T> issues a count to know totals; Slice<T> skips it.

questions.explanation: Use Slice (or keyset) for infinite scroll and when the count is expensive.

questions.prompt: Complete the Spring Data pagination vocabulary.
questions.text: A {1} knows the total number of elements and pages because it triggers a COUNT query; a {2} only knows whether a next slice exists; both are requested by passing a {3} such as PageRequest.of(page, size).
questions.explanation: Slice fetches pageSize + 1 rows to learn whether more exist. Use it, or keyset scrolling, for infinite scroll and for tables where COUNT is expensive.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which statements about Spring Data web pagination (a `Pageable` controller argument) are correct?

options.text: When the request omits `size`, the default `page` `size` is 20.
The `page` parameter is one-based by default.
options.why: It is zero-based by default; the one-indexed option must be switched on.

options.text: A requested `size` larger than the configured maximum is capped (2000 by default).
A `size` above the maximum makes Spring answer 400 Bad Request.
options.why: The `size` is silently reduced to the maximum rather than rejected.

options.text: The `page` parameter is zero-based unless `one-indexed-parameters` is enabled.
options.why: Index 0 is the first `page` by default, a classic off-by-one trap.

options.text: A `Slice` return type still runs a `COUNT` query to fill the totals.
options.why: `Slice` exists precisely to skip the `COUNT` query.

questions.explanation: Pair web pagination with a stable sort (a unique tiebreaker such as the id) or pages can overlap or skip rows.

questions.prompt: Entity `Post` has `createdAt` (`Instant`) and `id` (`Long`). In a Spring Data JPA `PostRepository`, declare a method named `next` that returns `List<Post>` and takes `Instant c`, `long i` and a `Pageable page`. Use a JPQL `@Query` for the keyset condition (`createdAt < c`, or equal `createdAt` with `id < i`), newest first with `id` as tiebreaker.

checks.label: keyset comparison on createdAt and id
order by createdAt desc, id desc

questions.explanation: Call it with `PageRequest.of(0, 21)` to fetch one extra row. Spring Data 3.1+ also offers built-in keyset scrolling (`ScrollPosition` and `Window`), which generates this query for you.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring `POST /payments` handler `pay(@RequestBody PaymentIn body, ...)` that reads the `Idempotency-Key` request header into a `String key`. A `ConcurrentHashMap<String, PaymentResult>` store exists: return the stored result for a repeated key, otherwise call `charge(body)` exactly once for that key and return its result.
questions.explanation: `computeIfAbsent` is atomic per key, so two simultaneous retries charge once. In production the store is a database table with a unique constraint (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) so it survives restarts and works across instances; also store a hash of the body to reject a reused key with a different payload.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring handler method `users()` for `GET /api/v1/users` returning `ResponseEntity<List<UserDto>>` from `service.all()`. Add the response headers `Deprecation` and `Sunset` (any plausible values) through the `ResponseEntity` builder.
questions.explanation: RFC 9745 defines `Deprecation` as a structured-field date ("@" plus a Unix timestamp) and RFC 8594 defines `Sunset` as an HTTP date. A servlet filter or interceptor can add the headers to a whole `/api/v1` prefix instead of every method.

questions.prompt: In a Spring for GraphQL `@Controller`, write a batch resolver for the `author` field of `Book`: method `author` takes `List<Book> books` and returns `Map<Book, Author>`, loading all authors with one call `authorRepo.findAllById(ids)` instead of one query per book.

checks.label: takes List<Book> and returns Map<Book, Author>
loads authors in bulk with findAllById (or findByIdIn)

questions.explanation: `@BatchMapping` wraps a `DataLoader` so the framework batches all `author` lookups for one request. A hand-registered `DataLoader` is the lower-level equivalent when you need more control.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query lists 25 books and resolves `author` for each book. Each `author` resolver does its own `SELECT`, and the books list itself is one `SELECT`. How many SQL statements run in total?
questions.explanation: 1 for the list plus 25 (one per book) is the N+1 problem. With a `DataLoader` or `@BatchMapping` the 25 `author` lookups collapse into one, giving 2.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A plain `@SchemaMapping` method `author(Book book)` is invoked once for every `Book` in the result list.
questions.reason: A `@BatchMapping` method receives all the `Books` of the request as one `List`.

whys.a: Wrong: R describes the fix, it is not the reason A happens.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but A happens because the field resolver is per parent object; R is how batching removes the repeated calls.

questions.explanation: Per-parent resolvers are the source of GraphQL N+1. Batch them with `@BatchMapping` or a `DataLoader` registered through `BatchLoaderRegistry`.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query asks for books and each book's author, and the author resolver throws for one book. What does a typical Spring HTTP GraphQL endpoint return?

options.text: HTTP 500 with an empty body, because the resolver crashed the request.
options.why: Field-level exceptions are caught by the engine and reported per field.

options.text: HTTP 404 for the missing author, as a REST controller would answer.
options.why: GraphQL has a single endpoint, so status codes do not map to fields.

options.text: HTTP 200 with partial data and an `errors` array.
options.why: Correct: GraphQL reports field errors in the body; the transport call itself succeeded.

options.text: HTTP 400 with a violations list like Bean Validation produces.
options.why: That body shape belongs to REST validation, not to GraphQL execution errors.

questions.explanation: Monitoring on status codes alone misses GraphQL failures; inspect the `errors` array and add a `DataFetcherExceptionResolver` for consistent error classification.

questions.prompt: What does registering Spring's `ShallowEtagHeaderFilter` for GET endpoints actually save?

options.text: Controller work, because a matching `ETag` stops the handler from running at all, so no queries execute.
options.why: The filter needs the response body to compute the hash, so the handler always runs.

options.text: Database queries, because the filter caches the result set between requests.
options.why: It keeps no server-side cache of results.

options.text: Bandwidth only: the controller still runs, then a matching `ETag` turns the reply into a 304.
options.why: Correct: the work is done, only the transfer is skipped.

options.text: Nothing, because Spring MVC cannot produce 304 responses on its own.
options.why: Conditional GET handling with 304 is supported by the filter and by `checkNotModified`.

questions.explanation: To skip the work as well, compute a cheap version (updated-at or a version column) and call `request.checkNotModified(etag)` before loading the data.
